newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's "Tiger" Azcarraga, media mogul, dies.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's "Tiger" Azcarraga, media mogul, dies.

text.p: Emilio Azcarraga Milmo, the media mogul who built Mexico's Grupo Televisa into the Spanish-speaking world's largest media firm, died on Wednesday from cancer, Televisa said. He was 66.

Azcarraga, whose death in Miami, Florida, came less than two months after he retired from Televisa, was a hard-nosed dealmaker who knew what audiences wanted to see, a knack that earned him billions of dollars and made him one of Latin America's richest men.

His critics said he oversaw a company whose insipid programming and pro-government news kept many Mexicans unaware of their country's troubles and glorified the decades-long rule of the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).
But whatever his politics, there was no doubting the business acumen of a man widely known as "The Tiger."

Although Televisa already dominated Mexico's media landscape when Azcarraga took over from his father Emilio Azcarraga Vidaurrieta in 1972, the company expanded its domain to eventually include four nationwide television networks, dozens of radio stations and magazines, music recording studios, cable television, several soccer teams and more.
Televisa became one of the world's largest producers of programming, making what has become its staple export to the world: Latin soap operas.
The soaps, with titles like "The Rich Also Cry," do not often have much to do with the average Mexican. Acknowledging this, Azcarraga defended the programmes as a means of escape for poor Mexicans.

"Mexico is a country that has a lot of screwed up poor, people who will not be able to escape their screwed up situation. Television has an obligation to entertain these people and let them escape from their sad reality," he reportedly said at a 1993 party to celebrate the program's success.

Social realism they are not. Televisa's soap operas eschew violence, corruption and sex and are mostly love stories geared toward family audiences. In a country where most people are dark-skinned, soap stars are usually light-skinned actresses.
The bulky billionaire did little to hide the cosy relationship his media company enjoyed with the government, which grants media licenses.

When accused once of helping the PRI during the 1994 presidential race by airing little positive news about the opposition, Azcarraga told reporters: "We are soldiers of the president of the republic, not the PRI."
And during a fund-raising banquet by former President Carlos Salinas in 1993, Azcarraga was widely reported by the Mexican media to have offered $50 million to help the PRI's re-election efforts.
Azcarraga did allow greater independence at Televisa in the last few years, giving wider coverage to opposition candidates and exposing some cases of government corruption.
Although he was seen as brash, Azcarraga shunned the public spotlight. He was famous for never having granted an interview since becoming head of Televisa.

There were even different theories as to why he was called "The Tiger." Some said it was a reflection of his business instinct, while others said it came from a grey flash that crowned his otherwise black head of hair.
A more likely explanation came from the fact that his father, Emilio Azcarraga Vidaurrieta, was known as "The Lion."
His 29-year-old son, Emilio Azcarraga Jean, took over the reins at Televisa on his father's resignation, in partnership with former chief financial officer Guillermo Canedo White.
He also has three daughters besides his son, and is survived by his fifth wife, Adriana Abascal.
